strengths: Establishes a novel and non-trivial theoretical equivalence (Thm 3.1) between two previously separate frameworks—mean-field (MF) theory of trainability and initial-guessing bias (IGB)—showing that key MF order parameters (signal variance/covariance) map directly onto IGB quantities (activation drift ratio, center variance) via a rigorous central-limit-theorem argument.

Derives a counter-intuitive but well-supported conclusion (Prop. 4.1) that the most trainable initialization is one of transient deep prejudice rather than neutrality, directly refining/correcting an open question left by prior IGB work (Francazi et al. 2024).

Identifies and corrects a subtle inaccuracy in prior MF literature regarding ReLU networks, showing that the correlation coefficient always converges to 1 across the whole phase diagram (persistent deep prejudice), with a careful closed-form derivation (App. G) of convergence rates (exponential vs. quadratic).

Extends both frameworks to previously unaddressed settings: non-zero bias variance in IGB, and multi-node activation functions (max/average pooling) in MF, providing new phase diagrams and practical initialization guidance for pooling-based architectures.

The theoretical development is detailed and mostly rigorous, with proofs of key lemmas/theorems in the appendix (e.g., using Stein's lemma, careful treatment of self-averaging, explicit recursive relations), and is validated against numerical simulations (Fig. 2, 7, 9) showing good agreement in the infinite/large-width regime.
The paper is reasonably self-aware about limitations, explicitly showing where finite-width networks deviate from the infinite-width theory (Appendix D) rather than hiding this discrepancy.
weaknesses: The practical significance of the central claim (optimal trainability requires transient prejudice) is not validated with actual training experiments (e.g., loss curves, convergence speed, accuracy) comparing EOC-initialized vs. neutral vs. ordered/chaotic networks; all validation is limited to signal-propagation statistics at initialization, leaving the connection to real trainability outcomes only theoretically argued.

Finite-width experiments (Appendix D, Fig. 6) show substantial deviation between MF/IGB theory and simulated finite networks, raising concerns about the practical applicability of the derived guidelines to realistically-sized networks.

All empirical validation is restricted to synthetic i.i.d. Gaussian data and generic MLPs (plus toy pooling extensions); no experiments on real datasets or more complex/modern architectures (CNNs, transformers) are provided, limiting evidence of broader impact despite claims that MLPs are 'building blocks' of complex models.

The fairness framing in the introduction and conclusion is somewhat superficial—while IGB is motivated by fairness concerns in prior work, this paper's contribution is essentially about trainability and phase diagrams, and it does not substantively engage with fairness metrics, discrimination across realistic class-imbalanced or structured datasets, or downstream fairness implications after training.

The paper's core contribution is primarily a formal/conceptual bridging of two existing frameworks (MF and IGB) rather than a fundamentally new theoretical tool or algorithm; the pooling-layer extension, while useful, is a relatively incremental application of existing IGB/MF machinery (via Hayou et al.'s Algorithm 1) to two specific pooling operations (max/average) with n=2 nodes.

The manuscript is dense and heavily reliant on appendices for essential proofs and derivations, which may hinder accessibility and independent verification by readers not deeply versed in prior MF/IGB papers.

Details on experimental setup (number of seeds, variance/error bars, exact dataset construction for Fig. 7's CIFAR10 gradient experiment) are sparse, making full reproducibility and statistical confidence in the empirical claims harder to assess.

strengths: The paper establishes a novel and rigorous theoretical equivalence (Thm 3.1) between two previously separate lines of work — mean-field (MF) trainability theory and the initial-guessing-bias (IGB) framework — showing that MF's signal variance/covariance map directly onto IGB's activation-drift quantities.

The derived counter-intuitive conclusion (Prop. 4.1) that optimal trainability corresponds to a state of 'transient deep prejudice' rather than neutrality is an interesting and non-trivial refinement of prior claims in [20].

The extension of the IGB/MF machinery to multi-node activation functions (max/average pooling) is a genuine, previously underexplored contribution, with concrete phase-diagram results (Fig. 4) and a lemma (E.3) characterizing when MaxPool preserves the EOC of the underlying single-node activation.

The paper corrects an overlooked detail in prior ReLU phase-diagram analyses (that the correlation coefficient always converges to 1 across the whole diagram, implying persistent deep prejudice), supported by explicit recursive derivations in App. G.
The theoretical derivations are detailed and mostly self-contained, with proofs, lemmas, and numerical verifications (Figs. 2, 5, 6, 7, 9) checking the theory against simulation.
weaknesses: All empirical validation is confined to checking theoretical formulas against synthetic i.i.d. Gaussian data and randomly initialized (untrained) MLPs; there is no actual training experiment demonstrating that the proposed 'optimal trainability' condition (transient deep prejudice at EOC) yields faster or more accurate learning in practice compared to alternative initializations, which is the central practical claim of the paper.

The paper's own finite-width experiments (App. D, Fig. 6) show that the MF/IGB correspondence breaks down substantially for realistic finite widths (width 50), raising doubts about the practical applicability of the theory outside the idealized infinite-width limit.

The framing around 'fairness' and 'prejudice' borrows loaded terminology from the algorithmic fairness literature, but the paper only addresses class-imbalance in classification outputs at initialization due to architecture on synthetic unstructured data — the connection to real-world fairness concerns (e.g., protected attributes, structured data bias) is tenuous and somewhat overstated in the introduction/conclusion.

The theoretical scope is restricted entirely to wide MLPs (explicitly acknowledged as a limitation); while pooling layers are included, there is no extension to more practically relevant architectures such as CNNs, residual networks, or attention-based models, limiting the significance of the contribution for modern deep learning.

The 'trainability' claims rest solely on gradient stability (χ̃₁) at initialization, without any discussion of how this relates to final model performance, optimization trajectory beyond the initial layers, or interaction with common practical techniques (batch norm, residual connections, adaptive optimizers) that are known to strongly affect trainability.

Several key theorems/lemmas are stated only informally in the main text with full proofs deferred to the appendix, and some derivations (e.g., in App. G) are lengthy and only cover ReLU, leaving other activations (e.g., leaky-ReLU, GELU used in practice) unaddressed.

No code or experimental reproducibility details (architectures, hyperparameter search, dataset preprocessing beyond CIFAR-10 standardization) are provided, making it hard to verify or reproduce the numerical results.

strengths: Establishes a rigorous theoretical equivalence (Thm 3.1) between two previously disconnected frameworks—mean-field (MF) theory of trainability and the initial-guessing-bias (IGB) framework of predictive fairness at initialization—providing a genuinely useful unifying lens for the field.

Derives a counter-intuitive but well-supported result (Prop. 4.1) that optimal trainability corresponds to a state of transient deep prejudice rather than neutrality, directly challenging a claim in prior work [20].

Identifies and corrects an oversight in prior MF literature regarding ReLU: the correlation coefficient always converges to 1 across the whole phase diagram, revealing persistent deep prejudice, which sharpens understanding of when 'c' is a valid order parameter for unbounded activations.

Extends IGB machinery to non-zero bias terms and to multi-node activation functions (max/average pooling), yielding new, practically relevant phase diagrams and an algorithmic recipe (via [12]'s Algorithm 1) for computing the EOC in these settings.

Provides fairly extensive theoretical derivations in the appendix (explicit ReLU recursions, gradient stability analysis, Stein's lemma-based calculations) plus empirical validation showing good agreement between IGB-predicted and MF-simulated correlation coefficients across depths, activations, and both synthetic Gaussian and CIFAR-10 inputs.
Clear framing of the paper's contributions and a coherent narrative connecting fairness/prejudice concerns to classical trainability theory.
weaknesses: The analysis is restricted to infinite-width MLPs; the paper's own appendix (App. D) shows that finite-width networks (width 50, depth 100) exhibit substantial deviations from the theory, and this gap is only acknowledged, not resolved, limiting practical applicability to realistic finite architectures.

The core equivalence theorem, while valuable as a unifying device, is largely a consequence of applying the central limit theorem to two known quantities under matched Gaussian-input assumptions; the paper could more clearly justify why this connection was non-obvious or technically difficult to establish previously.

Empirical validation is mostly restricted to synthetic i.i.d. Gaussian data (as required by the IGB derivation) plus one CIFAR-10 gradient experiment; there is no validation on realistic trained/training dynamics or more diverse datasets/architectures to substantiate claims about 'fast and accurate learning'.

The pooling-layer extension is demonstrated only for n=2 node pooling, which is a fairly narrow and non-representative case compared to typical pooling window sizes and modern architectures (CNNs, transformers) that the introduction motivates the work with.

The paper explicitly limits scope to MLPs and states extension to more complex architectures (CNNs, attention, normalization) as future work, so the practical significance for modern deep learning practice remains somewhat speculative.

Notation and proofs are dense (e.g., App. C, G), and the main text sometimes glosses over technical assumptions (e.g., simultaneous infinite-width and infinite-data limits) that could affect interpretability of the 'equivalence' claim for practitioners.

strengths: Establishes a rigorous and novel theoretical bridge between mean-field (MF) theory of trainability and the initial-guessing-bias (IGB) framework, unifying two previously separate lines of work with an explicit equivalence theorem (Thm 3.1/E.1).

The central result -- that the edge-of-chaos (best-trainability) initialization corresponds to a state of maximal (but transient) class prejudice rather than neutrality -- is a genuinely counterintuitive and interesting finding, with a clean theoretical proof (Prop 4.1) and supporting classification into ordered/transient/chaotic-deep-prejudice phases (Table 1).
Extends IGB to non-zero bias variances and to multi-node activation functions (max/average pooling), broadening applicability beyond the original single-node, zero-bias formulation.

Identifies and corrects a previously overlooked fact in the MF literature: for ReLU the correlation coefficient always converges to 1 across the whole phase diagram (with differing convergence rates), revealing persistent deep prejudice, which refines prior phase-diagram claims (e.g., Hayou et al.).
Extensive theoretical derivations (mean-field recursions, Stein's lemma arguments, explicit ReLU calculations) are carried out carefully and are largely self-contained in a lengthy appendix.

Fairly broad empirical validation across architectures (vanilla MLP, residual MLP, vanilla ViT, and a large pretrained ViT fine-tuned on CIFAR100) and datasets (binarized Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR10, CIFAR10, CIFAR100), with good qualitative agreement between IGB-predicted and MF-simulated quantities as network width grows.
weaknesses: The theory is restricted to the infinite-width, then infinite-data mean-field regime, where no feature learning occurs; this is acknowledged but substantially limits the practical relevance of the trainability claims to real, finite, feature-learning networks.

Several empirical demonstrations are weak in absolute terms (e.g., vanilla MLP reaches only ~50% test accuracy on CIFAR10), and the vanilla ViT experiments strip out normalization and skip connections specifically to preserve the theoretical phase structure, making these architectures unrepresentative of practically used models; this weakens the evidence that the theoretical predictions matter for realistic training regimes.

Framing the work heavily around 'fairness' and 'prejudice' is somewhat rhetorical/overloaded: the paper's notion of prejudice is purely about class-imbalance in random, unstructured, i.i.d. Gaussian input distributions at initialization, which has limited direct bearing on real-world fairness concerns (e.g., demographic bias, structured data); the societal-fairness framing in the intro/conclusion is not really substantiated by the technical content.

The core theoretical connection, while nontrivial to prove, is in some sense an expected consequence of combining two known results (the EOC has a stable fixed point c=1, and IGB relates c=1 to infinite γ i.e. deep prejudice); the paper could more explicitly discuss why this equivalence was non-obvious or what new predictive power it yields beyond reinterpretation.

Multi-class extension is only sketched via classification fractions in the binary case (Eq. 3); the general nc-class treatment is not fully developed in the main text, despite multi-class experiments (CIFAR10/100) being used for validation.

The large ViT experiment triggers phase behavior by uniformly rescaling all linear/conv weights by a single scalar factor, which is a coarse and somewhat artificial intervention that may not cleanly isolate the EOC/prejudice phenomenon from other confounds (e.g., interaction with pretrained normalization layers, biases left unscaled).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely interesting question: linking two previously separate literatures (mean-field theory of trainability and the initial-guessing-bias framework) under a unified formalism.

Theorem 3.1 (MF/IGB equivalence) and the accompanying derivations are carried out carefully, with detailed proofs in the appendix, and the extension of IGB to non-zero biases and multi-node activations (maxpool/avgpool) is a useful technical generalization.
The correction to prior claims about ReLU (showing that the correlation coefficient always converges to 1, contrary to earlier characterizations) is a concrete, verifiable technical contribution.

The empirical validation spans a reasonably wide range of architectures (MLP, residual MLP, vanilla ViT, and a large pretrained ViT) and datasets, showing qualitative consistency with the theoretical predictions of phase behavior.

The 'counterintuitive' framing (best trainability coincides with a biased rather than neutral initial state) is a potentially interesting conceptual message connecting fairness and optimization perspectives.
weaknesses: The central 'proof' of Proposition 4.1 in the appendix is essentially a restatement of already-known facts (EOC is optimal in MF; EOC corresponds to c=1 in IGB, hence prejudice) rather than a substantively new derivation — much of the paper's novelty rests on notational/parametric correspondence (Thm 3.1) between two frameworks that were already known to describe the same underlying signal statistics, raising questions about the depth of the contribution.

Empirical support for the central claim ('EOC is fastest to absorb bias and train') is largely qualitative (visual inspection of accuracy/max-frequency curves) without a quantitative metric (e.g., time-to-convergence, statistical tests) to substantiate 'fastest'.

Several reported experiments are weak in absolute terms (e.g., vanilla MLP reaching only ~50% test accuracy on CIFAR10), which undermines confidence in conclusions drawn about training dynamics from these architectures.

In the ordered-deep-prejudice phase, models sometimes reach performance comparable to EOC (attributed post hoc to optimizer/loss-landscape effects), which weakens the sharpness of the claimed distinction between phases.

The ViT experiments explicitly remove batch/layer normalization and residual connections to preserve phase distinctions, and the paper notes residual architectures have no order/chaos transition at all — this substantially limits the applicability of the theory to the normalization- and skip-connection-heavy architectures used in practice.

The analysis is restricted to the infinite-width, then infinite-data limit, explicitly excluding the feature-learning (proportional) regime, which the authors acknowledge as an important gap but do not address.

The connection to 'fairness' invoked in the introduction and motivation is fairly superficial; the paper does not explore practical implications or downstream fairness effects on real (non-random, non-Gaussian) datasets, despite this being one of the paper's stated motivations.
The manuscript is dense and notation-heavy, which may hinder accessibility and the ability of reviewers/readers to verify claims without extensive cross-referencing to the appendix.

strengths: Establishes a novel and rigorous theoretical bridge between two previously disconnected frameworks (mean-field theory of trainability and the initial-guessing-bias framework), with a clean equivalence theorem (Thm 3.1/E.1) mapping MF order parameters (q_aa, q_ab, c) onto IGB quantities (sigma_y^2, sigma_mu^2, gamma).

Derives a genuinely counterintuitive and well-supported conclusion: the edge-of-chaos (optimal trainability) initialization is a state of maximal (deep) prejudice rather than neutrality, directly countering an assumption in prior work [20].

Corrects an inaccuracy in prior MF literature regarding ReLU networks, showing the correlation coefficient always converges to one across the whole phase diagram (rather than only near specific regions), and carefully derives the two distinct mechanisms (ordered vs chaotic deep prejudice) with explicit convergence rates (Lemma H.1).

Extends the IGB/MF machinery to non-zero bias variances and to multi-node activation functions (max-pool, average-pool), broadening applicability beyond simple single-node activations and providing explicit phase-diagram shifts for these operations.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple architectures (MLP, residual MLP, vanilla ViT, and a large pretrained ViT fine-tuned on CIFAR100) and datasets (binarized FMNIST/CIFAR10, CIFAR10, CIFAR100), with good qualitative and quantitative agreement between theoretical predictions and finite-width simulations (including confidence-interval comparisons as width grows).
Very thorough appendix with detailed proofs, additional Lemmas, and extensive supplementary experiments, supporting reproducibility and rigor.
weaknesses: Results are confined to the strict infinite-width (then infinite-data) mean-field regime, where no feature learning occurs; the authors acknowledge this but it limits practical relevance to real, finite, feature-learning networks, and the extension to the proportional/finite-width regime is left as future work.

Empirical validation on more complex tasks is fairly weak: the vanilla MLP trained on CIFAR10 only reaches ~50% test accuracy, and the vanilla ViT (without normalization/skip connections) likely underperforms substantially compared to standard architectures, making it harder to assess whether the theoretical conclusions transfer to practically-relevant, well-performing models.

The large pretrained ViT fine-tuning experiment (Fig. 4 bottom, Fig. 13), while a nice attempt at realistic validation, shows somewhat noisier/less clean support for the central claim compared to the toy MLP experiments (e.g., favored-class accuracy behaves erratically for the ordered-deep-prejudice case), and only a single pretrained checkpoint/dataset is tested.

The framing of the contribution as connecting to "fairness" is a bit of a stretch: IGB's notion of class-frequency bias at initialization (on synthetic Gaussian data with balanced classes) is only loosely related to real-world fairness concerns about protected attributes and downstream discriminatory behavior; the paper does not empirically or theoretically engage with actual fairness metrics or real-world demographic bias.

The theoretical apparatus and notation are dense and heavily reliant on appendices; the main text sometimes glosses over derivations (e.g. Thm 3.1 stated only 'informally', full proof deferred), which may limit accessibility despite the paper's clarity efforts.

Most main-text training experiments focus on binary classification tasks derived by binarizing datasets (odd/even), with only limited true multi-class experiments (CIFAR10/CIFAR100), so the generality of the conclusions to genuinely multi-class, more realistic classification problems is only partially demonstrated.

No comparison against alternative or adaptive initialization schemes (e.g., data-dependent init, LSUV, other bias-correction strategies) that might mitigate the vanishing/exploding gradient problem without inducing deep prejudice, which would help contextualize the practical significance of the finding.
